gloss_terse: Rephaim — an ancient race of giants inhabiting Canaan and Transjordan before Israel's conquest
gloss_readable: A proper noun designating a pre-Israelite people renowned for their extraordinary stature. The Rephaim inhabited both sides of the Jordan: in Bashan, where Og was the last of their remnant (Deut 3:11), and in the valley south of Jerusalem that bears their name (2 Sam 5:18). Scripture links them with the Anakim and the Zamzummim (Deut 2:11, 20), painting a picture of formidable peoples displaced by divine mandate. German 'Totengeister' intriguingly echoes the homonymous connection to shades of the dead, though here the term is purely ethnic.

senses.1: The ethnic group Rephaim (רְפָאִים II), an ancient people of great physical stature who occupied Canaan and Transjordan before Israel's arrival. They appear in the Table of Nations context (Gen 15:20), in Og's kingdom of Bashan (Deut 3:11; Josh 12:4), and in the Valley of Rephaim near Jerusalem (2 Sam 5:18, 22). The name is distinct from the homonymous 'shades/dead' usage of the same root.

gloss_terse: To draw water from a well or spring; by extension, the person who draws water
gloss_readable: A verb describing the fundamental act of fetching water from a well, spring, or cistern. It appears memorably in the servant narratives at the well where Rebekah draws for Abraham's camels (Gen 24:19-45) and in the designation of the Gibeonites as perpetual 'drawers of water' (Josh 9:21). Isaiah employs it figuratively: 'You shall draw water from the wells of salvation' (Isa 12:3). Spanish 'sacar' (to pull out) and French 'tirer' (to draw) both capture the physical pulling action at the heart of this word.

senses.1: To draw or fetch water from a well, spring, or cistern, including participial forms denoting the person performing this task. The literal usage spans everyday life (Gen 24:11; 1 Sam 9:11; Ruth 2:9) and ritual contexts (1 Sam 7:6). Isaiah 12:3 extends it metaphorically to drawing salvation as one draws water, a striking figurative turn preserved across all major translations.

gloss_terse: Error, inadvertence — an unintentional sin as distinct from deliberate transgression
gloss_readable: A noun central to the Levitical sacrificial system, marking the boundary between sins committed unknowingly and those done with a 'high hand' (Num 15:25-29). Nearly every occurrence falls within Priestly legislation detailing the sin and guilt offerings required when someone errs without intent (Lev 4:2, 22, 27; 5:15, 18). The term also covers unintentional manslaughter in the cities-of-refuge legislation (Num 35:11, 15; Josh 20:3). Ecclesiastes borrows it to warn against careless vows (Eccl 5:5). French 'erreur' and Spanish 'inadvertencia' both preserve the nuance of accidental fault rather than willful rebellion.

senses.1: A sin or fault committed through ignorance, carelessness, or inadvertence rather than deliberate defiance. This is the technical term in Priestly law for unintentional transgression, triggering specific sacrificial remedies (Lev 4:2; 5:15; Num 15:25-29). It also governs the cities-of-refuge provision for accidental homicide (Num 35:11; Josh 20:3, 9), where the Deuteronomic parallel 'without knowledge' confirms its semantic core of unwitting error.

gloss_terse: Leg or thigh — the lower leg of a person or the upper hind leg of a sacrificial animal
gloss_readable: Refers to the leg as a body part, with a notable semantic split between human and animal contexts. For humans it denotes the lower leg or calf, as when Samson smites the Philistines 'leg upon thigh' (Judg 15:8) or in the lover's praise of marble-like legs (Song 5:15). For sacrificial animals it designates the upper hind leg or thigh — the priestly portion in the wave offering (Exod 29:22, 27; Lev 7:32-34). Spanish distinguishes these neatly: 'pierna' for the human limb, 'muslo' for the sacrificial thigh. The dual form appears for human legs (Deut 28:35; Prov 26:7).

senses.1: The physical leg or thigh of a person or animal. In human contexts it refers to the lower leg or calf, distinct from the thigh proper (Judg 15:8; Ps 147:10; Song 5:15). In sacrificial legislation it denotes the upper hind leg given to priests as their portion (Exod 29:22, 27; Lev 7:32-34; 1 Sam 9:24). Spanish translations helpfully distinguish 'pierna' (human leg) from 'muslo' (sacrificial thigh), reflecting the contextual semantic range.

gloss_terse: Truly, certainly — an adverb affirming the reality or genuineness of a statement
gloss_readable: An adverb derived from alethes ('true, unconcealed') that affirms the truthfulness or certainty of what is being said. It appears at critical moments of recognition in the Gospels — the centurion's confession 'Truly this was God's Son' (Matt 27:54; Mark 15:39) and the disciples' declaration after Jesus walks on water (Matt 14:33). Peter's Galilean accent is identified 'truly' by the bystanders (Matt 26:73). German 'wahrhaftig' and French 'vraiment' both emphasize genuine, verified truth rather than mere emphasis.

senses.1: An adverb meaning 'truly, certainly, indeed,' used to affirm the reality of a claim or identity. In the NT it marks decisive confessions of faith or recognition — the centurion at the cross (Matt 27:54; Mark 15:39), the disciples in the boat (Matt 14:33) — as well as assertions of verified fact (Matt 26:73; Mark 14:70). Cross-linguistically stable across all major translations as a marker of genuine affirmation.

gloss_terse: Antioch — a city name referring either to Syrian Antioch or Pisidian Antioch
gloss_readable: The proper noun Antiocheia designates two distinct cities in the NT. Syrian Antioch (modern Antakya, Turkey) served as the launching point of Paul's missionary journeys and the place where believers were first called 'Christians' (Acts 11:26). Pisidian Antioch in Asia Minor was a key stop on Paul's first journey, where he delivered a major synagogue address (Acts 13:14) and later faced persecution (Acts 14:19; 2 Tim 3:11). Paul's confrontation with Peter at Antioch (Gal 2:11) underscores Syrian Antioch's theological significance as the Gentile mission's home base.

senses.1: The city of Antioch (Ἀντιόχεια), referring to either Syrian Antioch — the major metropolis where Gentile Christianity flourished and where believers were first called Christians (Acts 11:26) — or Pisidian Antioch in Asia Minor, a stop on Paul's first missionary journey (Acts 13:14; 14:19). Spanish 'Antioquía' and French 'Antioche' preserve the classical name across translation traditions.

gloss_terse: Revelation, disclosure — the divine unveiling of hidden truth or eschatological reality
gloss_readable: From apo ('away') and kalypsis ('covering'), this noun denotes the uncovering of what was concealed — divine truth, a person's true nature, or end-time events. Simeon calls the infant Jesus 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles' (Luke 2:32). Paul uses it for the disclosure of God's mystery kept secret through the ages (Rom 16:25) and for the future revealing of Christ and the sons of God (Rom 8:19; 1 Cor 1:7). It also titles the final book of Scripture. French 'révélation' and German 'Offenbarung' both capture the sense of making openly known what was previously hidden.

senses.1: The act or event of divine disclosure — the unveiling of what was previously hidden, whether a specific spiritual truth, a person's identity, or eschatological realities. Paul employs it for the mystery of the gospel now revealed (Rom 16:25; Eph 3:3), for the future manifestation of Christ and believers (Rom 8:19; 1 Cor 1:7; 2 Thess 1:7), and for prophetic insight granted in worship (1 Cor 14:6, 26). Luke 2:32 applies it to Christ as light disclosed to the nations.

gloss_terse: Number — a count, total, or numerical quantity of persons or things
gloss_readable: A straightforward noun denoting a numerical count or sum. In Acts it frequently quantifies the growth of the early church — 'the number of men came to about five thousand' (Acts 4:4) — and the size of various groups (Acts 5:36; 6:7; 11:21). Revelation uses it symbolically for the number of the beast (Rev 13:17-18) and the count of angelic hosts or the redeemed (Rev 5:11; 7:4; 9:16; 20:8). The word is remarkably stable across languages: Spanish 'número,' French 'nombre,' and German 'Zahl' all render it directly.

senses.1: A number, count, or numerical quantity, whether literal or symbolic. In Acts it tracks the measurable growth of the believing community (Acts 4:4; 6:7; 11:21) and the size of movements (Acts 5:36). In Revelation it takes on symbolic force: the number of the beast (Rev 13:17-18), the 144,000 sealed (Rev 7:4), and the innumerable angelic hosts (Rev 5:11). John 6:10 uses it for the practical headcount of the five thousand fed by Jesus.

gloss_terse: Asia — the Roman province in western Asia Minor, with Ephesus as its capital
gloss_readable: In the NT this proper noun refers not to the modern continent but to the Roman province of Asia in western Asia Minor, centered on Ephesus. Paul was initially prevented from preaching there (Acts 16:6) but later spent years in Ephesus so that 'all who dwelt in Asia heard the word' (Acts 19:10). The seven churches of Revelation (Rev 1:4) are all located within this province. Asian Jews appear at Pentecost (Acts 2:9) and later accuse Paul in Jerusalem (Acts 21:27; 24:19). French 'Asie' and German 'Asien' retain the classical geographic reference.

senses.1: The Roman province of Asia (Ἀσία), encompassing western Asia Minor with Ephesus as its principal city. It is the region of Paul's extended ministry (Acts 19:10, 26), home to the seven churches of Revelation (Rev 1:4), and the origin of Jewish pilgrims at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). The Spirit initially forbade Paul from entering Asia (Acts 16:6), making his eventual prolonged work there all the more significant.

gloss_terse: Blasphemy, slander — profane or reviling speech, especially against God
gloss_readable: Denotes speech that profanes the divine name or defames another's reputation. Jesus teaches that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is the one unforgivable sin (Matt 12:31; Mark 3:28-29), setting this word at the heart of a grave theological warning. The high priest tears his robes at what he calls Jesus' blasphemy (Matt 26:65; Mark 14:64). Paul lists it among vices to be put away (Eph 4:31; Col 3:8). In Revelation it characterizes the beast's arrogant speech against God (Rev 13:1, 5-6). Arabic 'tajdif,' German 'Lästerung,' and Spanish 'blasfemia' all preserve the sense of sacrilegious reviling.

senses.1: Speech that profanes, reviles, or slanders — directed either against God (blasphemy proper) or against human beings (defamation, reviling). Jesus' teaching on the unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit (Matt 12:31; Mark 3:28-29) gives this term its sharpest theological edge. It also appears in the high priest's charge at Jesus' trial (Matt 26:65), in vice lists urging believers to put away abusive speech (Eph 4:31; Col 3:8), and as characteristic of the beast's defiance in Revelation (Rev 13:1, 5-6).
